density curve: A smooth curve where the area underneath represents probability and the total area equals one.
describing distributions: Summarizing a distribution by its shape, outliers, center, and spread (the SOCS framework).
dotplots, histograms, stemplots: Graphs for displaying quantitative data, each suited to different sample sizes and detail levels.
inverse normal: Finding the data value x that corresponds to a given percentile in a normal distribution.
mean: The arithmetic average of values; sensitive to outliers, unlike the resistant median.
modified boxplot: A boxplot that displays outliers as separate individual points beyond the whiskers.
observational study vs. experiment: Studies observe subjects without intervention, while experiments impose treatments and can establish causation.
skewed distributions: Asymmetric distributions where the mean is pulled toward the longer tail away from the median.
standard deviation: A measure of spread giving the typical distance of values from the mean; sensitive to outliers.
standardizing: Converting a value to a z-score using z = (x − μ)/σ to compare across distributions.
uniform distribution: A distribution with a flat density curve where equal-width intervals have equal probability.
confounding variable: A variable associated with both the explanatory and response variables, obscuring the true relationship.
connection between r and r²: In simple linear regression, the coefficient of determination R² equals the correlation r squared.
describing scatterplot: Summarizing a scatterplot by its direction, form, strength, and any outliers.
high-leverage point: An observation with an extreme x-value that can strongly influence the regression line.
identifying association: Detecting a relationship between variables when conditional distributions differ across categories.
influential point: An observation that, if removed, substantially changes the regression line or correlation.
interpreting slope: The predicted change in the response variable for each one-unit increase in x.
outlier in residuals: A point with a large residual that the regression line fits poorly.
pearson r: A measure of the strength and direction of a linear association, ranging from −1 to +1.
power model: A model fit by regressing log(y) on log(x), in contrast to the exponential model's log(y) on x.
residual plot: A plot of residuals where random scatter indicates a good linear fit.
simpson's paradox: When the direction of an association reverses after combining grouped data.
three explanations for association: An observed association may be due to causation, a common cause, or chance.
blinding: Concealing treatment assignment from subjects (single-blind) and/or evaluators (double-blind) to reduce bias.
block design: Grouping similar experimental units into blocks before randomly assigning treatments within each block.
cluster: A sampling method that divides the population into groups and randomly selects entire groups.
matched pairs: The simplest block design, pairing similar subjects or using before-and-after measurements.
randomization, replication, control: Three principles of good experiments that reduce bias, increase reliability, and limit confounding.
scope of inference: Random sampling permits generalization, while random assignment permits causal conclusions.
stratified: A sampling method that divides the population into strata and takes a simple random sample within each.
undercoverage, nonresponse, response bia: Sources of survey bias from excluded groups, unanswered surveys, and untruthful or skewed responses.
voluntary response: A self-selected sample that tends to overrepresent people with strong or extreme opinions.
b: The conditional probability formula P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B).
combining normal random variables: When X and Y are normal, their sum X + Y is also normally distributed.
complement rule: The probability an event does not occur equals one minus the probability it does: P(Aᶜ) = 1 − P(A).
four binomial conditions: The BINS requirements: binary outcomes, independent trials, fixed number n, and same probability p.
gambler's fallacy: The mistaken belief that past results change probabilities in future independent trials.
geometric vs. binomial: Both count successes with fixed probability, but the geometric setting has no fixed number of trials.
independence: Two events are independent when knowing one occurred does not change the probability of the other.
lln: The Law of Large Numbers: as sample size grows, the sample proportion approaches the true probability.
transformations: Linear transformation rules: E(aX+b) = aE(X)+b and Var(aX+b) = a²Var(X).
center: The mean of the sampling distribution of p̂ equals the true population proportion p.
central limit theorem: For large n, the sampling distribution of the sample mean is approximately normal regardless of population shape.
independence condition: Sampling without replacement requires the population to be at least ten times the sample size.
large sample condition: For normality of a proportion, both np ≥ 10 and n(1−p) ≥ 10 must hold.
larger n: A larger sample size produces a smaller standard error, giving more precise estimates.
normal/large sample condition: Inference for means requires n ≥ 30, a normal population, or no strong skewness.
random condition: Inference requires data from a random sample or a randomized experiment.
t-distribution: A bell-shaped distribution with heavier tails, used when σ is unknown, with n−1 degrees of freedom.
unbiasedness: A statistic is unbiased when its expected value equals the parameter it estimates.
variability: The spread of an estimator; a smaller standard error means a more precise estimate.
why the clt works: Averaging many random values concentrates the distribution, making the mean approximately normal.
10% condition: Sampling without replacement is valid when the sample is at most 10% of the population.
ci for p₁−p₂: A confidence interval for a difference of proportions using separate, unpooled sample proportions in the SE.
confidence level as long-run capture rat: The percentage of confidence intervals from repeated samples that would capture the true parameter.
connection between ci and two-sided test: A parameter falling outside the confidence interval corresponds to rejecting the null hypothesis.
interpreting ci: Stating that we are, say, 95% confident the true parameter lies within the calculated interval.
normal condition: For a proportion test, both np₀ ≥ 10 and n(1−p₀) ≥ 10 using the null value p₀.
one-sample: A procedure comparing one group's statistic to a known or hypothesized standard.
p-value: The probability of getting the observed statistic or something more extreme, assuming the null is true.
p-value interpretation: The probability of results this extreme or more extreme, assuming the null hypothesis is true.
test for p₁=p₂: A test for equal proportions using a pooled combined proportion in the standard error.
test statistic: z = (p̂ − p₀)/√(p₀(1−p₀)/n), using the null value p₀ in the standard error.
two-sample: A procedure comparing the statistics of two independent groups.
type i error: Rejecting a true null hypothesis; its probability equals the significance level α.
type ii error: Failing to reject a false null hypothesis; its probability is denoted β.
effect size measures: Quantities like Cohen's d or confidence interval width that gauge the practical magnitude of an effect.
power analysis: Determining the sample size needed to detect a given effect with a desired probability.
s/√n: The denominator of the one-sample t statistic t = (x̄ − μ₀)/(s/√n), with n−1 degrees of freedom.
sample size calculation: Finding n for a desired margin of error using n = (z*σ/ME)².
statistically significant: A result with p < α; distinct from practical significance, which requires a meaningful effect size.
t-interval: A confidence interval for a mean computed as x̄ ± t*(s/√n).
two-sample t-interval: A confidence interval for a difference of means: (x̄₁ − x̄₂) ± t*(SE).
two-sample t-test for μ₁ − μ₂: A test comparing two population means using Welch or conservative degrees of freedom.
when t-procedures are not appropriate: When the sample is small and the data show strong skewness or outliers.
interpreting: Giving plausible values for the rate of change in y per one-unit change in x.
interpreting p-value: The probability of getting a slope this steep or steeper by chance if the true slope were zero.
residual plot checks: Verifying a random pattern, constant spread, and no outliers to confirm regression conditions.
